about: The antiphon that opens Mass is a verse of the very psalm about to follow — its fourth (Ps 42:4). The psalm is framed by a line lifted out of its own middle — the shape Roman psalmody has taken for centuries. The Latin “gladdens my youth” follows the Greek translation: the Hebrew has two words for joy at that point and none meaning youth. This whole block of prayers began as the priest's private preparation; the missal of 1570 printed it at the head of the order of Mass.

s01.narrative: The priest stands at the foot of the altar, makes the reverence due to it, and signs himself from forehead to breast. The first words of Mass are said aloud.

s02.translation: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

s03.narrative: With hands joined before his breast the priest begins the antiphon and the server answers. From here until he goes up to the altar the prayers alternate.

s04.translation: I will go in unto the altar of God.

s05.translation: To God, who gladdens my youth.

w001.function: It governs the ablative: not “to the name” but “in the name” — in it and by its power.

w003.function: A genitive depending on “nómine” (w002). One preposition covers three genitives: one name, three Persons.

w007.function: 4th declension: one form serves for nominative and genitive alike. That this is the genitive is shown by “Sancti” (w008) and by the two genitives just before it.

w010.function: Future, not present: he has not gone in yet. The verb is built from intro (inwards) and ire (to go) — the priest announces what he is about to do.

w012.function: Accusative after “ad” (w011) — motion toward. The bare form could be nominative, accusative or vocative; the preposition settles it.

w013.function: Genitive: the altar belongs to God. Compare “Deum” (w015) — the same word in the accusative, because there he is the goal of the journey and not its owner.

w016.function: Nominative, though its antecedent “Deum” (w015) stands in the accusative: a relative takes its case from its own clause, and here it is the subject.

w018.function: The point where the Latin follows the Greek rather than the Hebrew: the Greek psalter has “youth” here, the Hebrew two words for joy.
